chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from one of his companions, from Al-Husayn ibn Al-Mukhtar, from Abu Usamah, from Humran, from Abu Ja'far عليه السلام, who said:

Indeed Allah, Mighty and Majestic, surely attends to the believer with affliction just as a man attends to his family with gifts during absence, and He protects him from the world just as a physician protects the sick person.

key_terms.الدُّنْيَا: the worldly life and its attractions from which the believer may be shielded
key_terms.الطَّبِيبُ: the physician, whose protective restraint serves as the comparison
key_terms.اللَّهَ: Allah, the Exalted, the one acting toward the believer with wisdom and mercy
key_terms.الْغَيْبَةِ: absence, referring to a man sending gifts while away from his family
key_terms.الْمَرِيضَ: the sick person who is prevented from harmful things for his well-being
key_terms.الْمُؤْمِنَ: the believer who is the subject of divine care through trials
key_terms.الْهَدِيَّةِ: a gift, used here as an analogy for deliberate and caring attention
key_terms.بِالْبَلَاءِ: through affliction or trial, as a means of divine tending

ai.seo_question: Why does Allah test the believer with afflictions and keep him from worldly things?
ai.summary: This hadith teaches that affliction for the believer is not abandonment, but a form of divine care and attention. It also shows that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, may withhold worldly ease from the believer as a mercy, just as a physician prevents a sick patient from what would harm him.
